To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
cynicism, but not exhaustion, is a significant predictor of performance.
job resources and cynicism predict team performance, whereas job demands and exhaustion do not.

(1) job demands are positively related to exhaustion and cynicism; (2) job resources are negatively related to exhaustion and positively related to cynicism; (3) exhaustion is not related to team performance, whereas cynicism is negatively related to team performance.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of burnout in explaining the relationship between working conditions and team performance.
a central assumption of the JD-R model: that job demands and job resources evoke different processes, which in turn influence performance in different ways.
a constructive replication of a well-established model in the field of occupational psychology.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
cynicism is the only burnout component that is associated with objective team performance.
the JD-R model is not supported as a model of objective team performance, but that the model is supported as a model explaining the relationship between job characteristics and attitudinal burnout.
job demands and resources predict performance via burnout, but that this relationship differs for the two components of burnout.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
job demands and job resources are important for performance.
job resources and cynicism are the most important predictors for team performance.
job demands, job resources and burnout (cynicism) all contribute to explaining variance objective team performance.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the Job Demands-Resources Model (Bakker and Demerouti 2007) is an effective framework for understanding the impact of job characteristics on employee performance, and that the model's assumptions can be tested empirically.
the Job Demands and Resources (JD-R) model, a popular framework in organizational behavior, can be used to explain the relationship between objective performance and job demands and resources.
the Job Demands-Resources model can be used as a framework to predict team performance.
